source_acquisition.search_note: The automated source inventory reports no_public_source_found and no local visual-source row exists. I verified the author-linked project page and mdyao/PhotoAgent with gh: the default code branch contains only README while the main branch contains rendered images but no figure/table generator, notebook or TeX. The arXiv source package for 2602.22809 contains camera_ready.tex, cvpr.sty and the exact PDF crop asset for every Figure, plus all six tabular captions/rows, so the status is exact_visual_source. RE-N-Y/imscore is recorded only as the footnoted metric implementation.

paper_style.palette_strategy: Three local palettes: colorful hand-drawn cyan/pink/green/orange pipeline diagrams; natural-color Input/Output photo montages with black labels; and black/white horizontal-rule tables with bold/underline ranking. Color carries important aesthetic/phase meaning in diagrams and photos, while table structure is mostly grayscale-safe.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: The main PDF is two-column and vector-first for text, rules, captions and imported PDF diagram paths, but every qualitative montage and many diagram icons are embedded raster images. Appendix one-column figures mix raster photos with vector labels; the final PDF is mixed rather than a pure plot-rendering document.
paper_style.style_consistency: Float/caption placement and Input/Output or method-column labeling are stable. The paper has strong local consistency within flow diagrams, photo galleries and tables, but font families differ across embedded assets (Nimbus/Computer Modern, ComicSansMS/Segoe/DengXian, TimesNewRoman). There are no uncertainty marks in any Figure and only point/percentage values in Tables.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1. PhotoAgent autonomously performs high-level, semantically meaningful edits aligned with human aesthetic, moving beyond low-level color, contrast, or illumination tweaks. Upper-Left: People-loop, where users iteratively inspect the image, propose edits, and apply changes until satisfied. Upper-Right: PhotoAgent, where the process runs autonomously. Bottom: Edited photos. Note that PhotoAgent also supports user-guided editing (Fig. 6).

color.semantic_mapping: Pastel issue boxes encode people-loop barriers; ring segments label Perceiver/Planner/Executor/Evaluator; arrows and status text encode the autonomous loop; Input/Output photo pairs encode visible edits.

encodings.shape: rounded boxes, icons and ring segments
encodings.facet: people-loop vs agent-loop plus three photo pairs
encodings.text: barrier text, candidate actions, Score/rollback and Input/Output labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Conceptual system overview plus three representative before/after photo pairs; it does not encode an aggregate success rate, editing-round distribution or sample denominator. The upper diagram distinguishes user expertise/algorithm/interaction barriers from the Perceiver–Planner–Executor–Evaluator loop, while the lower photos illustrate color/lighting changes.
figures.evidence_relation: Introduction barriers and autonomous-editing claim → Figure 1 overview → §3 four-component loop → Figure 2 detailed MCTS path → Figure 4/T1/T2 quantitative and qualitative evidence. The caption points to Figure 6 for user-guided editing; the examples are mechanism evidence, not population statistics.
design_strengths: Combines problem framing, architecture and visible outputs in one reading direction.
Component labels, arrows, status text and photo pairs provide redundant visual cues.
The caption explicitly separates people-loop, agent-loop and bottom results.
design_weaknesses: High information density and small hand-drawn labels in a double-column float.
Selected photos do not establish general performance or reduced user burden.
Pastel category colors are only partly robust in grayscale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a problem→closed-loop components→same-input/output headline canvas, but attach sample denominators, prompt metadata and a quantitative pointer.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2. Detailed loop of PhotoAgent. First, Perceiver extracts semantic cues from the current image and proposes N candidate editing actions. Second, Planner explores the candidate actions through iterative rollouts, scoring, and pruning to progressively refine edits and select the action that achieves the optimal result. Then, the executor applies these edits while the evaluator scores intermediate results, invoking re-planning when the score is unsatisfactory.

color.semantic_mapping: Perceiver, Planner, Executor and Evaluator use cyan, pink, green and yellow regions; arrows, score/rollback and the right-hand MCTS tree encode data flow and search.

encodings.text: candidate actions, Score, Rollback, Top-K and depth labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Method architecture diagram. It shows N candidate actions, a reduced-resolution lightweight loop, a depth-3 illustrative search tree, top-K filtering and re-planning, but no measured branching factor, simulation count or runtime. It is an interface to Algorithm 1 rather than an empirical plot.
figures.evidence_relation: §3 formulation of autonomous editing → Figure 2 component/data-flow map → Algorithm 1 MCTS pseudocode → Appendix Table 3 sim-to-real and Table 6 budget sweep. It operationalizes the loop that later produces the T1/T2 and Figure 4 results.
design_strengths: The central loop and right-side tree expose both system architecture and long-horizon search.
Stage colors, numbered arrows and direct labels make the main path recoverable without a legend.
design_weaknesses: Tree, tool icons and rollback arrows are crowded at double-column scale.
Illustrative depth and score labels can be mistaken for measured settings.
Caption omits K, resolution and budget definitions.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a main-loop diagram with a separated search inset and explicit visual distinction between measured hyperparameters and illustrative branches.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3. Pipeline for constructing the UGC-Edit Dataset and training reward model. We start with a diverse pool of source images from LAION and RealQA. Each image is processed through a structured prompt with Qwen3-VL for UGC classification. The images are then filtered by human annotators. Finally, a reward model is trained via GRPO to predict fine-grained quality scores.

color.semantic_mapping: Cyan cloud headers mark dataset/reward stages; source, VLM, human verification, policy/reference/reward models and green checks distinguish pipeline roles.

encodings.text: 7k+, authentic UGC, normal distribution, reward rates and advantages

figures.data_and_statistics: Two conceptual pipelines: source images from LAION/RealQA pass through Qwen3-VL classification and human filtering to 7k+ authentic UGC, then images feed GRPO reward-model training and group-advantage computation. The figure has no split sizes, label histogram, rejection counts, held-out n or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: §4 UGC-Edit/reward-model design → Figure 3 provenance map → T1 UGC Score and T4 PARA correlation → Figure 2 Evaluator and T2 user study. It makes the evaluator/data dependency visible without claiming that the green checks are statistical guarantees.
design_strengths: Dataset curation and reward training are shown together, linking data provenance to the evaluator.
Two parallel rows and icon/arrow language are easy to scan.
design_weaknesses: Filtering loss, train/test split and human-label protocol are invisible.
Check marks and distribution sketches may overstate validation.
Dense icon/text mix and color-coded model roles reduce grayscale clarity.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a two-row source→human-check→reward pipeline with retained/rejected counts, label scale and held-out split alongside the icons.

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4. Qualitative results. PhotoAgent generates visually pleasing edits by autonomously improving color harmony, composition, and aesthetic expressiveness, often introducing a stronger sense of visual dynamics and atmosphere. Baseline methods tend to produce incomplete or less coherent outputs.

color.semantic_mapping: Natural image color encodes the visual edit; fixed method labels and row/column positions redundantly encode comparison, while black gutters separate cells.

figures.data_and_statistics: Four representative photo scenes (person at sunset, horse/snow, llama and baby) are shown for six methods: Input, SDXL, InstructPix2Pix, GPT-4o, ReAct (cls.) and Ours. The montage has no image-level score, prompt, sample denominator or failure frequency; perceived harmony/composition is qualitative.
figures.evidence_relation: T1 aggregate metrics and T2 user study → Figure 4 matched visual cases → Figure 5 iterative process and Figure 6 user-guided cases. It illustrates the claim that Ours makes more coherent changes, but cannot establish that claim over all 1,017 test images.
design_strengths: Fixed scene rows and method columns enable direct within-case comparison.
Labels and repeated input tiles make content preservation inspectable.
Caption states both the intended visual dimensions and baseline contrast.
design_weaknesses: Curated examples have no sampling rule or blind evaluation.
Different color grading can be mistaken for quality and is not independently measured.
Six columns make photo details and method names small.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use an input-fixed qualitative matrix with a stable method order, but attach prompts, sampling strata and blind human/metric summaries.

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5. The editing process of our PhotoAgent over three iterations.

color.semantic_mapping: Photo pixels encode tone, object and atmosphere changes; fixed Input/Iteration-1/2/3 labels encode temporal order.

figures.data_and_statistics: Two selected editing trajectories with three iterations each: a sunset/person example and a food/plate example. No per-iteration action text, evaluator score, stop probability, sample count or uncertainty is shown; the strip is a qualitative process illustration.
figures.evidence_relation: F2 closed-loop design and termination text → Figure 5 intermediate states → T1 metrics and Figure 4 final qualitative comparison. It supports the possibility of sequential tone/object edits, not a general trajectory distribution.
design_strengths: Temporal strip makes multi-step editing visible rather than only showing final output.
Repeated labels and fixed tile positions make before/after sequence easy to follow.
design_weaknesses: Only two hand-picked sequences and no metadata for each transition.
Caption does not name the actions or score-based retention rule.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use Input→intermediate→final strips with each action, score delta and stopping decision attached to the corresponding transition.

figures.label: Figure 6

color.semantic_mapping: Prompt fragments in orange/black label high-level intent; photo tone/lighting encodes the generated atmosphere; column position encodes each prompt variant.

figures.data_and_statistics: Six user-guided mood/atmosphere prompt examples across two scenes. The image grid is a qualitative prompt-to-edit demonstration, not a user-study sample or prompt sweep; it has no success rate, content-preservation score or participant judgment.
figures.evidence_relation: Figure 1 caption’s user-guided pointer → Perceiver high-level intent → Figure 6 prompt/output pairs → T2 user preference. It demonstrates flexible input language but does not measure consistency across prompts.
design_strengths: Prompt text is colocated with its visual result.
Fixed two-row layout allows style differences to be compared quickly.
design_weaknesses: Prompts are truncated poetic fragments and each has one output.
Caption gives no prompt protocol or evaluation criterion; typography is small.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair an abstract intent string with input/output and report prompt-set coverage, human preference and content preservation.

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7. More visual results of PhotoAgent.

color.semantic_mapping: Natural photo pixels encode visual enhancement and preservation; paired tile position and Input/Output labels provide the structural key.

figures.data_and_statistics: Three additional before/after cases (flowers/food, spiral stairs and presenter) from the author’s visual-results asset. No prompt, action, score, sample frame, metric or uncertainty is included.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix D expands Figure 4 qualitative coverage; its examples are compatible with the T1/T2 claims but add no independent aggregate evidence.
design_strengths: Multiple scene types and clear paired labels expand qualitative coverage.
Large page-width photos preserve detail better than main double-column montage.
design_weaknesses: Generic caption provides no task or selection metadata.
A small gallery cannot establish generality or failure frequency.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a labeled gallery only as qualitative supplement, with case metadata and an explicit sampling protocol.

figures.label: Figure 8

caption.text: Figure 8. More visual results of PhotoAgent.

color.semantic_mapping: Natural photo appearance encodes editing outcomes; horizontal Input/Output pairing is the redundant comparison cue.

figures.data_and_statistics: Additional PhotoAgent before/after cases covering sunset architecture, snowboarding/person, street subject, hand-heart and seaside silhouette. They are illustrative outputs without prompts, score, denominator, repeated runs or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix D gallery follows the main qualitative and user-guided results; it visually supports broad scene coverage but not quantitative robustness.
design_strengths: Consistent paired structure makes changes easy to locate.
Multiple environments broaden the visible scene vocabulary.
design_weaknesses: Caption is repeated and gives no task, prompt or sampling frame.
Large aesthetic changes may reflect selective presentation rather than average behavior.
figures.reusable_pattern: Keep an appendix gallery structurally consistent with the main grid and add scenario labels, prompt and failure inclusion rules.

figures.label: Figure 9

caption.text: Figure 9. Comparison with closed-source advanced image editing models nano-banana2 and Grok-Imagine. While both can further enhance input images, Grok-Imagine tends to over-enhance, producing exaggerated or dreamlike effects (e.g., a background resembling lens flare), whereas nano-banana2 is more restrained but lacks clear aesthetic guidance (e.g., unnecessary sky edits). Our method preserves the original content when the image is already visually appealing.

color.semantic_mapping: Four fixed columns encode Input, Nano-Banana2, Grok-Imagine and Ours; image pixels encode over-enhancement, sky edits and content preservation.

figures.data_and_statistics: Two paired scenes compare two closed-source editors and Ours against Input. The caption makes qualitative judgments about over-enhancement and content preservation; there is no fixed prompt/API version, per-image score, sample denominator or user-study statistic.
figures.evidence_relation: §5.4 comparison claim → Appendix D Figure 9 external-editor cases → T1 metrics/T2 user study and Figures 10–12. It supplies failure-mode exemplars for competing editors, not a controlled full benchmark comparison.
design_strengths: Four-column order keeps external methods and Ours directly comparable.
Caption names distinct failure modes rather than merely saying “better.”
design_weaknesses: Closed-source model versions and prompts are not reproducible.
Two curated cases cannot support prevalence or a general ranking.
Color/atmosphere judgments are subjective and lack blind scoring.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use an Input + external baselines + Ours grid with fixed prompts, version metadata and a paired blind preference summary.

figures.label: Figure 10

caption.text: Figure 10. Nano-banana2 tends to add excessive details and may alter the main subject, such as the llama in the figure. Grok-Imagine often over-enhances and introduces unnecessary flares. Our method avoids unnecessary changes when the input image is already visually appealing (e.g., the cat) and produces more aesthetically pleasing results.

color.semantic_mapping: Model columns encode the comparison; cat/llama subject pixels and flare/background changes encode unnecessary detail and preservation.

encodings.text: Input, method names and Ours labels

figures.data_and_statistics: Two animal cases target main-subject alteration and unnecessary detail/flare. The visual claim is example-level; no object-preservation metric, prompt, model version, sample size or uncertainty is supplied.
figures.evidence_relation: Figures 9–10 extend §5.4 closed-source comparison and Appendix G failure boundary; they complement T1/T2 but do not quantify “unnecessary changes.”
design_strengths: Subject identity stays visible across four columns.
The two cases target concrete failure types rather than only overall aesthetic preference.
design_weaknesses: Selective examples and caption rhetoric can amplify differences.
No operational definition of “unnecessary” or independent annotation is provided.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a no-op/high-quality-input stress set with a measurable content-difference threshold and blind human labels.

figures.label: Figure 11

caption.text: Figure 11. Our method generates images that preserve the original content and creative intent while enhancing the overall artistic mood and sense of atmosphere.

color.semantic_mapping: Four model columns encode the comparison; photo pixels encode content preservation and sunset mood enhancement.

figures.data_and_statistics: One seaside person scene compares Input, Nano-Banana2, Grok-Imagine and Ours. The caption states content/creative-intent preservation and mood enhancement, but no prompt, score, human rating, image n or uncertainty is reported.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix D’s content-preserving comparison → Figure 4 qualitative alignment and T1 CLIP/UGC metrics. It is a single qualitative mediator example, not evidence of broad intent preservation.
design_strengths: Single scene makes the content-versus-atmosphere trade-off easy to inspect.
Fixed four-column order matches Figures 9–12.
design_weaknesses: A single selected case cannot support a general preservation claim.
No action/prompt metadata or independent content-difference measurement.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair a content-preservation metric with a fixed four-column mood example and report cases where preservation fails.

figures.label: Figure 12

caption.text: Figure 12. Our method generates images with richer texture and material quality, while also enhancing the overall atmosphere and artistic mood, surpassing other compared methods.

color.semantic_mapping: Four model columns encode comparison; texture, material, atmosphere and light are carried by photo pixels.

figures.data_and_statistics: One dog/airport-luggage scene compares Input and three methods. The caption claims richer texture/material and atmosphere, but the figure has no prompt, score, sample denominator or uncertainty; “surpassing” is example-level.
figures.evidence_relation: Complements T1 quality metrics and Figures 9–11 with a material/texture case; it does not independently validate the UGC reward model.
design_strengths: Same subject and fixed method order isolate texture/lighting differences visually.
Large tiles retain detail useful for qualitative inspection.
design_weaknesses: Single case and uncontrolled color/lighting changes can look like quality gain.
Caption makes a broad comparative claim without a quantitative or human-evaluation link.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a same-subject material-quality grid with blind ratings and objective content/texture checks across a sampled set.

figures.label: Figure 13

caption.text: Figure 13. Some failed results where the editor may have made excessive changes.

color.semantic_mapping: Input/Output positions encode before/after; excessive subject/background/color changes encode failure cases in natural photo pixels.

figures.data_and_statistics: Three explicit failure examples (tiger, elephant and bird scenes) illustrate excessive or undesirable changes discussed in Appendix G. There is no failure denominator, taxonomy frequency, prompt, model version or uncertainty; this is boundary disclosure, not a failure-rate plot.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix G failure paragraph → Figure 13 counterexamples → terminate-condition discussion and the positive galleries F4/F7–F12. It narrows the broad “consistent” claim by showing where the system can over-edit or mismatch expectations.
design_strengths: Placing failure cases after positive galleries gives the reader visible boundary evidence.
Input/Output pairs and varied scenes make the error modes concrete.
design_weaknesses: Three cases do not estimate occurrence or conditional risk.
Caption does not identify which case is dark/low-quality, high-quality no-op or expectation mismatch.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair success galleries with a failure strip classified by trigger and report full-set failure rates and stop decisions.

tables.label: Table 1

caption.text: Table 1. Quantitative comparison of different planning strategies. The best results are in bold, and the second best are underlined.

tables.uncertainty: Each row is an aggregate point estimate over the 1,017-photo editing benchmark; no image-level n beyond the dataset description, seed/run dispersion, uncertainty or failure count is shown.
tables.data_and_statistics: Eight methods are compared on CLIP Similarity↑, ImageReward↑, BRISQUE↓, Laion-Reward↑ and UGC Score↑. PhotoAgent is best on CLIP 0.6254, BRISQUE 0.6217 and Laion-Reward 0.5134; GPT-4o is best on ImageReward 0.4115 and UGC Score 4.210. The four 0.x metrics use four decimals while UGC Score uses three; arrows define direction.
tables.evidence_relation: Main results claim → Table 1 aggregate metrics → Figure 4 qualitative grid and Table 2 vote share; T4 validates the UGC reward model externally and T5/T6 quantify cost/budget. The table shows metric-specific wins rather than an all-metric sweep.
design_strengths: Direction arrows and bold/underline immediately expose best and second-best.
Row blocks separate GPT-4o, single-step baselines and multi-step strategies.
Several metrics and UGC-specific score preserve multiple decision dimensions.
design_weaknesses: Wide six-column table is compressed by 0.9 textwidth.
No uncertainty, split, prompt, hardware or image-level denominator is shown.
UGC Score and automatic metrics may reward different properties, so aggregate rankings are not a single quality axis.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a multi-metric comparison with explicit direction and best/second-best, while adding dataset n, split, repeatability and metric provenance.

tables.label: Table 2

caption.text: Table 2. User study results: percentage of votes selecting each method as the best.

tables.uncertainty: Vote shares from 20 participants × 27 scenarios = 540 votes; no participant-level variance, scenario-level counts, tie rule, prompt protocol or uncertainty interval is displayed.
tables.data_and_statistics: One body row gives best-vote percentages: HuggingGPT 12.6%, ReAct (cls.) 15.2%, GPT-4o 30.2% and PhotoAgent 42.0%. Values sum to 100.0% and are rounded to one decimal.
tables.evidence_relation: T1 automatic metrics and Figure 4 qualitative comparisons → Table 2 human preference check → abstract/conclusion “user study” claim. It covers four methods only, not every T1 method.
design_strengths: Extremely compact single-row table makes the 42.0% share easy to locate.
Method labels align with the qualitative comparison vocabulary.
design_weaknesses: Caption omits the stated 540-vote denominator and participant/scenario design.
No disagreement or confidence information and only four methods are tested.
tables.reusable_pattern: Report vote share with participant/scenario n, per-scenario aggregation and participant-level uncertainty.

tables.label: Table 3

caption.text: Table 3. Consistency between simulated (low-resolution) rewards and full-resolution rewards.

tables.uncertainty: Top-1/Top-3 retention and Spearman/Kendall correlations are point summaries without candidate-pool n, repeated resolution draws, seed, uncertainty or pixel-size details.
tables.data_and_statistics: Four rows compare 1/2 versus 1/4 resolution: Top-1 retention 85%/75%, Top-3 retention 100%/90%, Spearman 0.94/0.79 and Kendall τ 0.90/0.73. Percentages and correlations use mixed precision.
tables.evidence_relation: F2 reduced-resolution MCTS simulation → Table 3 sim-to-real ranking check → full-resolution top-K rescoring and closed-loop replanning prose. It bounds the approximation claim; 1/4 resolution is not perfect alignment.
design_strengths: Places retention and rank correlation side by side for two resolutions.
Small table is readable and directly tied to the design question.
design_weaknesses: No action count or sampling protocol makes the denominator opaque.
Mixed percentages/correlations can be overinterpreted as one common accuracy measure.
tables.reusable_pattern: Pair resolution levels with retention and rank metrics, and include candidate n and paired sampling details.

tables.label: Table 4

caption.text: Table 4. Correlation of the reward model with human judgments on the PARA dataset.

tables.uncertainty: PLCC/SRCC are point correlations without PARA sample n, split, bootstrap/seed uncertainty or same-table PIAA baseline values.
tables.data_and_statistics: Aesthetic and Content columns report PLCC 0.7390/0.7577 and SRCC 0.7560/0.7702. Four decimal places are used. The table measures reward-model alignment, not end-to-end editing quality.
tables.evidence_relation: Figure 3 UGC reward training → Table 4 external PARA correlation → T1 UGC Score and evaluator claim. It supports external alignment but not the full PhotoAgent pipeline.
design_strengths: Two target dimensions and two correlation families fit in a very small table.
Four-decimal values preserve ranking precision.
design_weaknesses: No n, confidence, split or baseline value; “generalization” is difficult to audit.
Content/aesthetic correlations are not directly linked to user-study preference.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a metric×label-dimension correlation table with n, split, uncertainty and external baseline rows.

tables.label: Table 5

caption.text: Table 5. Runtime breakdown of PhotoAgent under the default configuration.

tables.uncertainty: Approximate seconds and percentages from one default profiling pass; no hardware, parallelism, network/API latency, repeated measurements, image n or uncertainty. Footnote excludes initialization and duplicated evaluator time.
tables.data_and_statistics: Rows decompose Perceiver ∼10s/2.1%, Planner (MCTS) ∼250s/53.2% of total and 100% of parent, nested Executor ∼170s and Evaluator ∼80s, top-level Executor ∼180s and Evaluator ∼30s, Total ∼470s/100%. Percentage uses total/parent semantics and one decimal.
tables.evidence_relation: F2 architecture and Algorithm 1 → Table 5 component latency → Appendix F optimization directions and Table 6 simulation budget. It supplies a practical efficiency boundary rather than a formal cost guarantee.
design_strengths: Nested parent percentages expose where planner time is spent.
Total and component rows give an actionable optimization map.
design_weaknesses: Approximate values and mixed parent/total denominators are easy to mis-sum.
Hardware, concurrency and evaluator duplication assumptions are outside the table.
tables.reusable_pattern: Report component time with explicit denominator, hardware, measurement repetitions and end-to-end wall-clock definition.

tables.label: Table 6

caption.text: Table 6. Impact of simulation budget on accuracy and runtime.

tables.uncertainty: A single simulation-budget sweep reports point metrics; no seed/run dispersion, image n, hardware, memory or uncertainty. Time is approximate seconds and metrics use different directions/scales.
tables.data_and_statistics: Five, ten, fifteen and twenty simulations give ∼60/∼120/∼185/∼250s; BRISQUE 0.6292/0.6270/0.6246/0.6217, Laion-Reward 0.5083/0.5099/0.5103/0.5134, UGC Score 3.982/4.005/4.121/4.176. Time and the three quality columns use mixed precision; arrows mark direction.
tables.evidence_relation: §5.3 simulation-budget ablation → Table 6 quality/runtime trade-off → Table 5 default profile and T1 quality metrics. It is the strongest numeric planning-budget check, but does not quantify depth=1 or evaluator removal.
design_strengths: Runtime and three quality metrics are aligned in one sweep.
Monotone rows make the quality–latency trade-off easy to inspect.
design_weaknesses: Caption says accuracy although two columns are reward/quality proxies.
No repeatability or cost-normalized quality and no depth sweep.
tables.reusable_pattern: Use a budget sweep with quality direction, measured wall time, hardware and run/image-level uncertainty.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 frames people-loop barriers and the autonomous loop → Figure 2 expands Perceiver/MCTS/Executor/Evaluator and rollback → Figure 3 supplies UGC-Edit/reward provenance → Table 1 and Figure 4 compare methods/visual outputs → Table 2 adds user votes → Figures 5–6 show iterative and user-guided behavior → Appendix Tables 3–4 validate simulation/reward alignment → Figures 7–12 expand positive and external-editor cases → Tables 5–6 expose runtime/budget trade-offs → Figure 13 discloses failure boundaries.
cross_object_system.caption_system: All captions use the printed Figure/Table number followed by a period and sit below the object. F1–F3 describe setup and components, F4/T1/T2 are result-oriented, F5–F8 are short labels, F9–F12 contain stronger comparison claims, and F13 is a failure caption. Captions rarely state sample n, prompt/model version, aggregation, uncertainty or protocol, so almost every montage and table requires body text.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: Horizontal hlines without vertical rules form the shared table grammar. T1 uses wrapped two-level metric headers and bold/underline best/second-best; T2 is a one-row vote table; T3/T4 are metric-by-condition tables; T5 uses total/parent nested percentages; T6 aligns simulation count with time and three quality metrics. No table has a dedicated uncertainty/failure column.
